paras: The Uniontown camp meeting shooting was a fight on Sunday, September 4, 1881, in which white "roughs" attacked Black attendees of a colored camp meeting near Uniontown, Fayette County, Pennsylvania. Thomas Gilbert, a Black man, was shot and thought fatally wounded, several others were shot or cut, and one Black man was chased four miles and shot in the back.

The camp meeting had been held near Moore's Works during the preceding week. According to a same-day Uniontown dispatch, a fight broke out that afternoon between "some white roughs" and the camp's Black attendees, and Clark Sweeny, a white laborer, shot Gilbert in the thigh. "The greatest uproar" followed, a number of shots were fired, and several other people were hurt, none as badly as Gilbert.

A correspondent writing from Uniontown three days later said the meeting "broke up Sunday night" in a row with "white rowdies" in which several were shot and others cut. He added that "the whites came out victorious" and that one Black man was chased four miles and "finally shot in the back."
No later report of Gilbert's condition or of any arrest appears in the coverage.

The New York Sun printed the dispatch on September 5 as "Shooting Affray at a Colored Camp Meeting," naming the wounded man and the shooter. The New-York Tribune gave it one line in its news digest: "A negro was shot at a camp meeting near Uniontown, Penn."

The Morgantown New Dominion's correspondent "Alexis" mentioned the row on September 17 at the end of a letter about railroad building and land sales. He called the Black participants "darkies" and framed the outcome as a contest the whites had won.

The same-day dispatch placed the fight in the afternoon, while the later letter put it on Sunday night. Neither account says whether Gilbert, shot in the thigh, and the man shot in the back were the same person.

reader.title: Uniontown camp meeting shooting
bases: A group of white men described as 'roughs' or 'rowdies' fought Black attendees at a camp meeting, shooting and cutting several of them and chasing one man four miles before shooting him; no death was reported (A1, A3).

A Uniontown telegraphic dispatch (A1, summarized in A2) and an independent correspondent's letter written from Uniontown three days later (A3) agree that a fight between white men and Black attendees at a colored camp meeting near Uniontown on Sunday, Sept. 4, ended with several people shot; they differ on the hour and on which victim they describe.

accounts.label: Uniontown telegraphic dispatch
accounts.gist: On the afternoon of Sept. 4 a fight between white roughs and Black camp attendees led to the shooting of Thomas Gilbert by Clark Sweeny and the wounding of several others amid 'the greatest uproar'.

accounts.label: Morgantown paper's correspondent
accounts.gist: The camp meeting near Moore's Works broke up Sunday night in a row between Black attendees and 'white rowdies'; several were shot and cut, the whites 'came out victorious', and one Black man was chased four miles and shot in the back.

framing.detail: The Sun ran the dispatch under 'Shooting Affray at a Colored Camp Meeting', describing the white attackers as 'roughs' and naming both the wounded man and the shooter.
The Tribune reduced the story to one line, 'A negro was shot at a camp meeting near Uniontown, Penn.', in its daily news digest.

The New Dominion's correspondent mentioned the row in passing in a letter about railroads and land sales, calling the Black participants 'darkies' and the whites 'rowdies', and reporting that 'The whites came out victorious'.

conflicts.note: The dispatch was sent the same day from Uniontown and is the more immediate source; the letter was written three days later and may describe the end of the disturbance rather than its start.
